title: ABA Model Rule 5.3: Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance, with Official Comments
pub: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct
author: American Bar Association

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The Rule supports the cluster’s emphasis on human accountability and context-sensitive, risk-based oversight, while materially grounding those principles in professional duties governing external and internal nonlawyer assistance. It does not itself establish AI’s jagged capabilities or task-level productivity effects.
qs: A lawyer must give such assistants appropriate instruction and supervision concerning the ethical aspects of their employment, particularly regarding the obligation not to disclose information relating to representation of the client, and should be responsible for their work product.
When using such services outside the firm, a lawyer must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the services are provided in a manner that is compatible with the lawyer’s professional obligations.

st.t: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
st.an: Rule 5.3 directly supports the cluster’s distinction between continuing supervisory duties and automatic liability. It requires reasonable managerial and supervisory safeguards, makes external-provider oversight context-sensitive, and limits responsibility for specific misconduct to ordering, knowing ratification, or knowing failure to take timely remedial action.
qs: including the education, experience and reputation of the nonlawyer; the nature of the services involved; the terms of any arrangements concerning the protection of client information; and the legal and ethical environments of the jurisdictions in which the services will be performed, particularly with regard to confidentiality.

st.t: Technology competence: Delegation preserves professional responsibility
st.an: The Rule 5.3 comments directly support the cluster’s proposition that outsourcing does not displace professional responsibility. They require circumstance-sensitive direction and monitoring of outside nonlawyers, while allowing monitoring responsibility to be agreed with a client subject to additional legal obligations.
qs: When retaining or directing a nonlawyer outside the firm, a lawyer should communicate directions appropriate under the circumstances to give reasonable assurance that the nonlawyer's conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the lawyer.

[4]  Where the client directs the selection of a particular nonlawyer service provider outside the firm, the lawyer ordinarily should agree with the client concerning the allocation of responsibility for monitoring as between the client and the lawyer.

kp.k: Managers must establish safeguards for nonlawyer conduct
kp.d: Rule 5.3(a) requires partners and lawyers with comparable managerial authority to make reasonable efforts to maintain firm measures reasonably assuring that nonlawyers’ conduct is compatible with lawyers’ professional obligations.
qs: shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm has in effect measures
compatible with the professional obligations of the lawyer

kp.k: Supervising lawyers must oversee nonlawyer compliance
kp.d: Rule 5.3(b) separately places a reasonable-efforts duty on lawyers who directly supervise nonlawyers, whether those nonlawyers operate within or outside the firm.
qs: a lawyer having direct supervisory authority over the nonlawyer
shall make reasonable efforts

kp.k: Lawyers can bear responsibility for nonlawyer misconduct
kp.d: Under Rule 5.3(c), a lawyer is responsible for qualifying nonlawyer conduct when the lawyer orders or knowingly ratifies it, or when a manager or direct supervisor knows in time to avoid or mitigate consequences but fails to take reasonable remedial action.
qs: ratifies the conduct involved
fails to take reasonable remedial action

kp.k: Internal assistants require ethical instruction and supervision
kp.d: Comment [2] states that employees and independent contractors assisting legal practice require appropriate ethical instruction and supervision, particularly concerning confidentiality, and that lawyers should take responsibility for their work product.
qs: appropriate instruction and supervision concerning the ethical aspects of their employment
should be responsible for their work product

kp.k: Supervision reflects nonlawyers’ training and disciplinary status
kp.d: Comment [2] says supervisory measures should account for nonlawyers’ lack of legal training and their absence from the professional disciplinary system applicable to lawyers.
qs: they do not have legal training
are not subject to professional discipline

kp.k: External technology services remain subject to professional duties
kp.d: Comment [3] permits lawyers to use outside nonlawyer services, including document-management, scanning and Internet-based information-storage services, but requires reasonable efforts to ensure that those services operate consistently with the lawyer’s professional obligations.
qs: using an Internet-based service to store client information
compatible with the lawyer’s professional obligations

kp.k: External-service oversight depends on contextual risk factors
kp.d: The required extent of oversight varies with the provider’s education, experience and reputation; the nature of the service; contractual protections for client information; and the legal and ethical environments where work occurs, especially confidentiality rules.
qs: education, experience and reputation of the nonlawyer
particularly with regard to confidentiality

kp.k: Lawyers should give external providers appropriate directions
kp.d: When retaining or directing an outside nonlawyer, the lawyer should provide context-appropriate directions designed to give reasonable assurance that the provider’s conduct complies with the lawyer’s professional obligations.
qs: a lawyer should communicate directions appropriate under the circumstances
give reasonable assurance

kp.k: Client-selected providers require monitoring responsibility allocation
kp.d: Comment [4] states that when a client chooses an outside nonlawyer provider, lawyer and client ordinarily should agree on responsibility for monitoring. Matters before tribunals may create additional legal obligations beyond the professional rules.
qs: the allocation of responsibility for monitoring
additional obligations that are a matter of law

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no explicit claims or predictions about AI changing legal services.
pts.d: The ABA sets out professional obligations regarding nonlawyer assistance within and outside law firms. Its examples include document management and Internet-based storage, but it does not discuss AI or predict technological effects on legal work, employment, or markets. Applying these provisions specifically to AI would be an interpretation beyond the supplied text.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source provides normative authority, not empirical evidence or an AI-specific argument.
pts.d: The document consists of ABA Model Rule 5.3 and its official comments, with cross-references to other professional-conduct rules. It supplies no AI data, benchmarks, cases, or findings. These are model provisions; the supplied text does not establish adoption by any particular jurisdiction.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: There is no AI adoption timeline or prediction horizon; the obligations are circumstance-dependent.
pts.d: The source is labeled 2026, but that is not a forecast horizon. For outside assistance, the extent of the obligation depends on the provider's background, the services, information-protection arrangements, and applicable legal and ethical environments. Responsibility under paragraph (c) depends on ordering or knowingly ratifying conduct, or specified managerial or supervisory authority combined with knowledge and failure to take reasonable remedial action.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The provisions address managers, supervising lawyers, nonlawyer assistants and outside providers, and clients—not AI-specific market segments.
pts.d: Partners and lawyers with comparable managerial authority must establish reasonable firm-level measures; direct supervisors must make reasonable supervisory efforts. Assistants require ethical instruction and supervision, particularly concerning confidentiality. When clients select outside providers, the comments ordinarily call for agreement about allocation of monitoring responsibility.
